A very depth(heh)-filled game that I'm really thankful that I had a second monitor for (and also my work place have a second monitor set up as well). So I can look at guide and wiki on the side.

Artstyle wise, about as you expect from this top down pixel art games. But I don't think people play Siralim for the creatures design or the story, but for the gameplay depth.

There's so many options, equipments, upgrades, etc. And it encourages you to try different team combination and fusion to see what the game could offer.

It's a lot to do. And the main story is really a long tutorial to unlock everything for the game as a whole. It is meant to play endless in the post-game, yeah. Which isn't the endgame, from what I read, seems there's more to do still.

I really enjoy my time with the game. Though I'm not as crazy over it as The Darkest Time or Guards II, since simpler is better sometimes for the brain. Mechanically deep is mechanically interesting, and it will be a kick of excitement for some.

Overall, a good game. Though not one I can spend hundred of hours over to 100%. BUT I can see and understand immensely people who're into Siralim full on will spend so much time with the game.

I like that I get to play it, once again, not a game I would ever usually get. But the experience is really fun for me. Thank ya, Lext.

I’d like to start by saying that I absolutely loved the game. Having said that, it’s been one of the strangest experiences I’ve ever had. That’s why, when I started looking for Q&As about the creation of Gorogoa, I found myself having to stop for a moment when I remembered his famous:

- Believe it or not, Eraserhead is my most spiritual film.
- Elaborate on that.
- No.

It also reminded me of what we call "literatura ascética" in Spanish. If there’s one thing I love, it’s reading. And this game, despite having no dialogue, felt just like reading the works of Fray Luis de León and Saint Teresa of Ávila. There are many games that have made me feel all sorts of different things, but with Gorogoa, once I’d finished it, I spent a couple of hours thinking about it. About its symbolism. And, to refer back to Lynch once more, some things you simply have to experience for yourself.

Game over. This was a tough game, not because of the mechanics (which are quite simple and, I’d go so far as to say, rather original in terms of the dialogue) but because of the themes it deals with.

The game warns you at every turn. You know what you’re getting yourself into. And, what’s more, you can check what elements are in each scene before playing it. And you do. Even though you know what’s coming, it tears you apart. Even though you know what’s coming, it still leaves you reeling. It doesn’t do so, however, by playing on your morbid curiosity. Such a sensitive subject is handled with great sensitivity, and when you watch the bonus scene, it all makes sense: some of the crew have experienced it first-hand.

I have to say that, personally, it has helped me. There are things from my childhood that I hadn’t dared to talk to anyone about and… there they are. I can’t change what happened to me, but I can talk about it with professionals. And without this game, I might never have dared to.
